idiom_name: java.util.function.Predicate + a generic @FunctionalInterface Filterer captured by a method reference
implementation_notes: The classic structure is already idiomatic Java: java.util.function.Predicate<T> is a first-class criterion with and/or/negate composition, and the container declares filtered() returning a generic @FunctionalInterface Filterer<G, E> { G by(Predicate<? super E> p); } whose implementation is captured by an instance method reference - 'return this::filteredGroup;' - so no Filterer class is ever written and the body is one stream().filter(predicate).collect(...) (or removeIf for in-place deletion). What replaces the classic structure is use-site variance: declaring Filterer<? extends Container, ? extends Element> filtered() lets subinterfaces narrow the element type covariantly, avoiding one xxxFiltered method per lower bound and per inheritance level. A hand-written Filterer implementation is still justified only where the criterion must carry more than one predicate or state, or on pre-Java-8 runtimes (anonymous inner classes).
pitfalls: Type erasure blocks the obvious design: by(Predicate<? super E>) cannot be overloaded and filtered() cannot be overridden with a narrower Predicate, which is precisely why the Filterer indirection with wildcards exists - dropping the wildcards silently removes the pattern's benefit.

Getting the variance direction wrong (Predicate<? extends E> instead of <? super E>) makes the method accept fewer criteria than before, and the error usually appears at the caller, far from the declaration.

Streams are lazy but the surrounding filtered() body usually materialises; returning a Stream instead leaks pipeline semantics (single use, no reuse) into the container's API - decide which contract you want.

Predicates are null-hostile by default (Predicate.isEqual(null), Objects.requireNonNull in combinators) and a criterion that throws mid-stream leaves no partial result, only an exception; test null elements explicitly if the container can hold them.
